units.text: How to Read a Study Without Turning It into a Verdict

A psychological finding can change how we judge a situation without delivering a verdict on every person in it. If an experiment shows that a particular pressure changes behavior on average, it does not follow that we know how a specific individual reacted. The group effect and the biographical explanation are different levels.

An experiment compares conditions constructed by researchers. Random assignment, when properly carried out and maintained, can help separate the intervention's effect from other differences between groups. But the conclusion remains tied to the intervention actually tested, the measurements used, and the population studied. After reading, we cannot expand the meaning of a narrow task into “human morality in general.”

Observational research examines differences in the existing world. It can identify important associations and attempt to account statistically for alternative explanations. Yet the fact that two characteristics vary together does not by itself establish causal direction or the absence of other causes. That is why the study of collective efficacy must not be read as a promise that a neighborhood will become safe if residents are simply encouraged to trust more.

A meta-analysis combines findings from several studies, but does not automatically turn their diversity into a universal law. We need to know what types of situations were included, how effects were measured, and how different the conditions are. The average can be useful while variation across contexts remains essential to a practical decision.

The absence of a detected difference also requires care. Simply stating it does not prove that two interventions are identical. The precision of the estimate and what the study was capable of detecting matter. When a study in this book found no differences on a dimension, that wording must not be expanded into a claim that the dimension cannot be influenced in any way.

There is also the question of the unit of analysis. A study of the probability that an individual will help answers a different question from one about the probability that at least one person in a group will intervene. Findings may seem contradictory if the reader shifts unnoticed from one question to the other. Sometimes an apparent controversy is, first of all, a confusion about what was measured.

Finally, a finding can be correct and still be misused. An average difficulty observed in a group does not justify withdrawing the rights of every member. A mechanism of obedience does not absolve every act committed under authority. An effect of material constraints does not turn a person into an object without initiative. Further arguments are needed between description and the moral treatment of people.

Responsible reading thus keeps two questions separate: “What do the data warrant believing?” and “What do we have reason to do in light of them?” The second needs the first, but is not fully contained within it.
